result.summary: Pausanias continues describing Polygnotus's painting of the sack of Troy at Delphi. He names the dead Trojans and Greeks shown, notes where the poet Lescheos differs from other tradition, and describes the house of Antenor, spared by the Greeks.

scenes.title: The dead of Troy
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the fallen figures in the painting and who killed them, citing Lescheos and other traditions.

scenes.title: House of Antenor spared
scenes.summary: The painting shows Antenor's family sorrowfully leaving their house, marked by a leopard skin. A couplet by Simonides names the painter.
scenes.stakes: Antenor's family faces exile after the fall of their city.

notable_quotes.reason: Simonides' couplet records Polygnotus as the painter of the Sack of Troy.

analysis.text: Pausanias compares the painting with epic sources, showing how myths varied between poets and how art preserved competing traditions.
The painting in the Cnidian clubhouse at Delphi by Polygnotus (5th century BC) was a celebrated work; Pausanias uses it to survey lost epics like those of Lescheos.

fun_facts.text: Lescheos, cited here, was the poet of the lost Little Iliad, which survives mainly through such quotations.

language_notes.text: Laver means a washing basin or trough; the painting shows one among the figures.
Mygdones was the name of a Phrygian people; Pausanias derives it from Mygdon, Corœbus's father.
Corœbus came to Troy hoping to marry Cassandra, Priam's daughter, and died in the sack of the city.
Household Zeus is Zeus as guardian of the home, whose altar stood in the palace courtyard.
Stesichorus was a lyric poet whose Fall of Ilium gave a version in which Hecuba was rescued by Apollo.
A leopard skin over the door marked the house as protected, because Antenor had favoured peace and the Greeks' envoys.
An elegiac couplet is a two-line verse form of a hexameter followed by a pentameter, often used for inscriptions.

context_notes.text: Lescheos is the author of the epic Little Iliad, which Pausanias often cites for details of Troy's fall.
Theano was a priestess of Athena at Troy and Antenor's wife; their sons were Glaucus and Eurymachus.
Polygnotus of Thasos was a famous fifth-century BC painter. This picture of Troy's sack was in the Lesche of the Cnidians at Delphi.

literary_notes.text: Showing the family's sorrowful faces gives Antenor's household pathos even though they are spared, so the sack's grief reaches both sides.
The ordinary details of the chest, the ass and the little boy make the scene of exile concrete and moving.
